questions.stem:
The names of the 400 employees of a company are listed alphabetically in a book.

The chairperson of the company wishes to select a sample of 8 employees.

The chairperson numbers the employees from 001 to 400

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Describe how the list of numbers can be used to select a systematic sample of 8 employees.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: Select a random number as the starting point
B1: Take every 50th employee
Notes: B1 for realising they need to select a random number as the starting point. B1 for realising they need to take every 50th employee.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) State one disadvantage of systematic sampling in this case.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) B1: e.g. The alphabetical list may not be random or May be biased as list not truly random or Some combinations of names are not possible
Notes: B1 for a suitable disadvantage. Sight of the words in bold oe for those reasons are sufficient provided there is no contradiction or not a correct reason. Condone "may not be representative". "some employees with the same surname won't be chosen". Do not allow any reference to requiring a sampling frame as it already has one e.g. "a sampling frame is needed because there is an alphabetical list"

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Write down the probability that the sample includes both the first name (employee 001) and the last name (employee 400) in the list.
(1)

questions.stem:
The volume of water in a bottle has a normal distribution with unknown mean, $\mu$ millilitres, and known standard deviation, $\sigma$ millilitres.

A random sample of 150 of the bottles of water gave a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$ of

$(327.84, 329.76)$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Using the confidence interval given, test whether or not $\mu = 328$

State your hypotheses clearly and write down the significance level you have used.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu = 328$   $\mathrm{H_1}: \mu \neq 328$ oe
dB1: Significance level is 5%
B1: (328 is within the interval therefore) no evidence to support that $\mu$ is not 328
Notes: Note that many are carrying out a full hypothesis test by finding the distribution of the sample mean. These three marks can still be scored. You do not need to check the calculations to score in (a). B1 for both hypotheses correct in terms of $\mu$ (do not accept use of $\bar{x}$). dB1 correct significance level given. Allow $(\alpha=)0.05$ Do not allow if more than one given. This mark is dependent on a two tail test being indicated with their hypotheses condoning slips in notation e.g. use of $\bar{x}$. Do not allow $p=0.05$ on its own. B1 idea that $\mu = 328$ is supported. Allow e.g. "do not reject $\mathrm{H_0}$" provided $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu=328$ but condone poor notation for their null hypothesis. Does not need to be in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A second random sample, of 200 of these bottles of water, had a mean volume of 328 millilitres.

(b) Calculate a 98% confidence interval for $\mu$ based on this second sample.

You must show all steps in your working.
(Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.)
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1 B1: $1.96 \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{150}} = \frac{329.76-327.84}{2} (=0.96)$ oe or e.g. $328.8+1.96\times\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{150}}=329.76$ or $328.8-1.96\times\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{150}}=327.84$   $[\sigma = 5.9987]$
M1 B1: $328-2.3263\times\frac{"5.9987"}{\sqrt{200}}$ oe or $328+2.3263\times\frac{"5.9987"}{\sqrt{200}}$ oe
dM1: $328 \pm 2.3263\times\frac{"5.9987"}{\sqrt{200}}$ oe
A1: $(327.0132\ldots, 328.986\ldots)$ (awrt 327, awrt 329)
Notes: M1 forms an equation to find $\sigma$. Allow $1.6<|z|<2$ may be seen in (a) or implied by awrt 6. B1 use of awrt 1.96 in the calculation may be seen in (a) or implied by their value for $\sigma$. M1 correct method to find one end of the confidence interval using their $\sigma$. Allow $2.3<|z|<3.1$ condone use of 150 rather than 200 (may be implied by awrt 327 or awrt 329 if no incorrect working is seen). B1 awrt 2.3263 seen. dM1 dependent on both the previous method marks being awarded. Fully correct method using their $\sigma$ and using n = 200 to find both ends of the confidence interval. A correct confidence interval with no working - send to review. A1 (awrt 327, awrt 329) Condone missing brackets.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Using five different random samples of 200 of these bottles of water, five 98% confidence intervals for $\mu$ are to be found.

(c) Calculate the probability that more than 3 of these intervals will contain $\mu$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: $X \sim \mathrm{B}(5, 0.98)$   or   $Y \sim \mathrm{B}(5, 0.02)$
A1: $\mathrm{P}(X\geqslant 4)$ or $\mathrm{P}(Y\leqslant 1) = {}^5C_4(0.98)^4(0.02)+(0.98)^5$ oe
$= 0.9961\ldots$   awrt 0.996
Notes: M1 use of Binomial e.g. B(5,0.98) or B(5,0.02) or $0.98^5$ or ${}^5C_x \times 0.98^x \times 0.02^{5-x}$ (may be implied by awrt 0.0922 or awrt 0.904 within a calculation or awrt 0.996). A1 for ${}^5C_4\times 0.98^4\times 0.02+0.98^5$ oe eg awrt 0.0922 + awrt 0.904 or implied by awrt 0.996. A1 awrt 0.996

parts.label: a
parts.reason: Spearman's rank correlation is not mentioned anywhere in the S statements; S5.1 only covers PMCC (product moment correlation coefficient) hypothesis testing, and S2.2/S5.1 explicitly exclude calculation involving correlation coefficients via formula but do mention PMCC via calculator, not Spearman's. Spearman's rank is a named concept not covered.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Hypothesis test using Spearman's rank correlation
parts.reason: Depends on Spearman's rank coefficient from part (a), which is out of spec; also no statement covers hypothesis testing with Spearman's rank (critical values table for rank correlation not mentioned).

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Rationale for using rank correlation over PMCC
parts.reason: This explanation relies on understanding Spearman's rank vs PMCC, a topic not in spec.

parts.label: d
parts.reason: Concept of tied ranks in Spearman's correlation, not covered by any statement.

parts.label: a
parts.reason: Chi-squared tests (goodness of fit) are not mentioned in any S statement; S2.4 explicitly says 'Significance tests, other than those mentioned in Section 5, will not be expected' and Section 5 only covers binomial proportion and normal mean tests, not chi-squared.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Expected frequency calculation for contingency table (chi-squared test of association)
parts.reason: Part of chi-squared test of association, not covered by any statement and excluded per S2.4.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Degrees of freedom for chi-squared test
parts.reason: Chi-squared test concept entirely absent from spec statements.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Two-sample z-test for difference of means
parts.reason: Hypothesis testing for difference between two population means is not covered; S5.3 only covers a test for the mean of a single Normal distribution, not two-sample tests. This is a distinct, unlisted technique.

parts.label: b
parts.reason: Relies on the out-of-spec two-sample hypothesis test framework from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.reason: question dropped: other parts out of spec

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Sum of independent Normal random variables
parts.reason: Normal distribution linear combination (sum of independent normals) is not covered by S4.2, which only covers the single Normal distribution as a model and finding probabilities, not combinations/sums of normal variables (a distinct technique not stated anywhere in the S statements).

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Difference of independent Normal random variables
parts.reason: Same issue as (a); linear combinations of normal distributions not in spec.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Linear combination of independent Normal random variables (G - 2T)
parts.reason: Same issue; combinations of normal random variables entirely absent from spec statements.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Central Limit Theorem applied to uniform distribution
parts.reason: Central Limit Theorem is explicitly excluded: S5.3 states 'Knowledge of the Central Limit Theorem or other large sample approximations is not required.' Also uniform distribution/continuous random variable mean-variance not covered.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Confidence interval using CLT result for uniform distribution parameter
parts.reason: Depends on the CLT-based distribution derived in (a), which is explicitly excluded per S5.3.
